utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and to the interpreters; good morning to the Prosecution. I see that you're all out in full force, and the Defence counsel as well. Good morning, General Krstic. We are running a little over an hour late. Why, Madam Registrar? Can you give us an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Apparently there was a problem with General Krstic's wheelchair and ... [French interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you. Mr. Petrusic, is there a problem with respect to General Krstic's health? Could you bring us up-to-date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The health problem of General Krstic is a constant one. It has been present for some time now, and I should like to state that before this Trial Chamber and the public. In the course of yesterday, General Krstic was to have had a medical examination, a medical checkup, because, according to General Krstic, he is experiencing the same problems he had 15 days ago when surgical intervention was performed on him. During the course of yesterday, for let me say technical reasons, that medical examination did not take place. I think the reason for it was problems with transport from the Detention Unit, and there was no electricity, as far as we were able to gather, at the Detention Unit. The information that General Krstic received from the administration of the Detention Unit, the medical examination has been rescheduled for Monday, and we'll know in the course of today whether it will indeed take place on Monday, whether we will continue the proceedings on Monday without the presence of General Krstic, who quite obviously is suffering from problems. He is experiencing problems. In the opinion of the Defence, and don't take this as too strong a word, but these problems will have to be dealt with. I cannot tell you the exact date at this point, but I think that it was some 20 to 25 days ago when he had a magnetic resonance examination. We still have not received any medical official findings, and we consider that it is essential for us to be able to -- for him to be able to receive the adequate therapy. It is a fact that General Krstic is having serious health difficulties and this would have to be dealt with for him to be present at these legal proceedings, and it is his wish, indeed, and his right and obligation, of course, to be present at his trial. The fact that he has been absent at times is exclusively due to his health, and we do expect all the medical staff and medical experts finally to come up with a diagnosis and, having come up with a diagnosis, the therapy that will improve the health situation of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. As you know, this is always an overriding preoccupation of ours. We would like to see things go well, and the Chamber, as you know, is always vigilant and always following the health situation of the General Krstic, and we have always recommended to the registrar that the utmost be done to ensure an improvement. To continue, let me say good morning to General Radinovic. You shall be continuing with your testimony. Let me remind you you are under oath once again, and you will be answering questions put to you by Mr. Andrew Cayley. Mr. Cayley, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours ... [French interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've made progress, Mr. Cayley, progress indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I still getting the French translation? No. I'm not. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, we left off yesterday where we were talking about the Krivaja 95 document, which we will leave for the moment, and we also spoke a little about the responsibilities of the Chief of Staff of a VRS corps, specifically the Drina Corps. What I'd like to do with you very briefly is to go through some of your testimony that you provided during Mr. Visnjic's examination-in-chief and just get you to confirm what you said. On the 6th of December, General, you said, and I quote, "It is only the Chief of Staff in the absence of the commander, by way of automatism, takes over the function of command, because according to the rules and regulations and according to the law, it is provided for the fact that he then acts as Deputy Commander, as Deputy Commander. So that provision is there so that in no situation whatsoever is there any discontinuity in command." Is that the correct position, both for a VRS Corps Chief of Staff and, indeed, the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You further said in your evidence, and again I'll quote, "When he," and you're referring to the commander, "is prevented from being on the spot, he does not have to write out an act or document designating a deputy, so the Chief of Staff on the basis of this automatic mechanism takes over in the absence of command." Is that also correct, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It need not be so, but it can be so, but it need not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When wouldn't that be the correct position?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is basically correct, but the commander for certain assignments can request that the Chief of Staff be authorised and be the de facto commander, which is what happened with the Zepa operation. He was appointed commander of the operative group and thus did not use his right of deputy. And this automatic mechanism of commanding when -- in the commander's absence, but he was appointed commander of the operative group, and in that way all dilemmas as to who was responsible for that operation was dealt with, null and void.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now let's talk about, specifically about Operation Krivaja 95 and the Drina Corps, and you said in your examination-in-chief, and you were referring here to General Krstic, and this is at page 8019, "And in his role at that post," referring to General Krstic, "was to plan the Operation Krivaja 95, and from the forward command post as Chief of Staff to supervise its implementation, the course of the operation." Do you agree with that statement, your own statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And finally you said two lines down, "In his role," again referring to General Krstic, "of Deputy Commander of the Drina Corps, General Krstic could have, when the Corps Commander was not around, then he could have realised the function of command." Do you stand by your statement, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the absence of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move now, General, to a different subject. You said in your evidence in-chief that as a matter of military convention, that attacking forces must normally always be much stronger than defending forces, and you said that normally an attacker should be seven to ten times stronger than a defender in terms of manpower. Is that a correct summary of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He need not be, but that is the ratio forces which ensures the certain taking over, taking control of towns which are well-fortified points of resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we take the situation in Srebrenica, what would your opinion be as an expert military man as to the multiple, the ratio, that should have applied in that particular case? How much stronger should the VRS forces have been than the Muslim forces within the enclave, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the assignment that the command of the Drina Corps had set in his order for active combat activities, active combat, in my view, the multiple, the ratio between the VRS and the Muslim forces in the enclave was 1:2.8 to the advantage of the Muslims. The question now arises --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whether I have calculated that properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've misunderstood my question. What I asked you, and it may well be that I didn't make it clear enough, in your professional opinion as a military man, what should, what should the ratio have been between the attacking force and the defending force? Not what it was in actual fact, but what should it have been?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take into account the fact that the Muslim forces in the Srebrenica enclave had more than two years, that is to say, a full two years to prepare for their defence, then we would be able to conclude that it was a good defence with all the rules applicable, shelters for the manpower; features for reconnaissance; for firing; bunkers for minefields; all other obstacles necessary for preparing settlements, settled outside the enclave, that is to say, outside the town proper on the boundaries of the enclave; resistance points for long-term defence; the preparation of the flanks and other positions; and everything that tactics implies for the preparation of towns or urban entities for defence purposes in order to prepare the proper kind of defence. And I can only assume that a trained command staff would pose as its objective the study and appraisal of the enemy which they were going to attack. And I think that all professional officers, all professional soldiers who know what warfare is, must have assumed that the 28th Division was well prepared in that way, had prepared its defence properly along those lines. And with that kind of situation, it was quite unrealistic to plan the taking over of the town. And regardless of the ratio that the army -- that is to say, the relationship of the army to the demilitarised zone and as a contracting party, it was not duty-bound to respect the status because the other side --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I'm going to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- went against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you're actually wandering away with your answer from the question that I asked, and I'll repeat it. In your opinion as a military man, what should, what should the ratio have been between the attacking force and the defending force? Now, you've laid out for the Judges that the Muslims were well dug in. They had very good defences. You're the General. You tell the Court what the ratio should have been between the attacking forces and the defending forces. If you can't answer the question, then just say, "I'm sorry, I don't wish to answer that question."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer it and I will answer it, but I'm just trying to tell you how we arrive at a ratio of forces. I did not say that the Muslim army or, rather, the 28th Division had prepared that kind of defence. I said that it should have prepared a defence of that kind, and that they would have had to assess the VRS in planning their operation. So in attacking a defence of that kind which they expected, which the officers of the VRS expected - at least the Command of the Drina Corps did - they must have had a ratio of forces which would guarantee the realisation of their assignment which could possibly include the liberation of Srebrenica. And this ratio should have been at least 5:1. The Drina Corps could not ensure those forces, let alone plan an operation of that kind, and that is why the order was compiled for active combat and not for an attack operation, because an attack operation would imply far greater forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, the 28th Division had between 8.000 and 10.000 men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my analyses, I had two types of sources in arriving at the figures that the 28th Division had. One of my sources were intelligence sources obtained by the army of Republika Srpska. That was one type of source. In that regarding, I had at my disposal a document sent by the Commander of the Milici Brigade to the Commander of the Drina Corps and some other intelligence sources which the corps collected itself. It is according to this data that the Milici Brigade, this intelligence information that the Milici Brigade sent, in the Srebrenica enclave, within the frameworks of the 28th Division, there was between 5.000 and 6.500 men. There were five brigades numbering -- depending on which brigade, but between 800 to 1.200. The 81st Brigade, for example, had 200 men. So along with these five brigades, we had the Diversionary Reconnaissance Battalion with about 550 men. Then we had the diversionary platoons within the brigades. And if you add all that up together -- there was a tank battery as well. And if we add all that together, that would make it somewhere between 5.000, 5.500 and 7.000, 7.500 men, depending on your calculations. I also sought out other documents as well, and I had at my disposal a series of documents originating from the Muslim side. According to those documents, and they were documents in which -- that is to say, documents from the staff of the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica via the operative groups right down to the 28th Division, informed its Superior Command about all the stages of the organisational and formative aspect of the army in Srebrenica, beginning with the autumn of 1991 when the Patriotic League was established as a party paramilitary in Srebrenica via the TO staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, excuse me. I don't want to go through the history of the Territorial Defence in Srebrenica. The number that you've given me is fine, 5.000 to 6.500 men. If, please, Exhibit 160 -- do you have your report handy, General? Do you have it with you, your report you produced on Srebrenica? It's Defence Exhibit 160. If you could please turn to page 25 in your edition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it's page 26. If page 26 could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could move it up, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if you could read paragraph 2.9 of your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Infantry Division consisted of the -- the 28th Infantry Division consisted of five brigades and a corresponding number of mountain and police units, the total numerical strength being between 10.000 and 12.000 men. The numbers of the brigades and the routes on which they were engaged were as follows: "The 280th Brigade on the route Potocari-Srebrenica. "The 281st Brigade on the route Podgaj-Borovac-Suceska. "The 282th Brigade on the route Zeleni-Jadar-Bojna-Srebrenica. "The 283rd Brigade on the route Podravno-Bucje-Viogora. "The 284th Brigade on the route Ravni Buljim- Milacevici-Potocari." Let me just say that the number of the brigades --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, read to the end of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. I just wanted to say that, in different documents, I came across different numbers for the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please read the paragraph to the end and then I'll ask you a question about these figures.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The mountain battalion and police forces were located in Srebrenica, Potocari, and Suceska in the role of the commander's reserve of the 28th Infantry Division. The total number of men under arms in Srebrenica amounted to between 12.000 and 13.000 combatants and armed policemen and members of various other paramilitary units stationed in Srebrenica at that time. "

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you would agree with me that there is a variance between your report, what you told Mr. Visnjic, and what you're now telling me, what you're now telling this courtroom in cross-examination. In your report, in the 28th Division, you say that there were 10.000 to 12.000; to Mr. Visnjic you said there were 8.000 to 10.000; and now to the court you're saying 5.000 to 6.500 men. Which is the correct figure, General? How many combatants were there within the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you'll have to be patient and hear my whole answer in view of the document. I said that I had at my disposal documents, intelligence documents of the units of the Drina Corps. The second type of document that I had at my disposal were the documents of the Muslim army. Those documents, as far as I know, as far as I know, the Defence sent to the Prosecution; and as far as I know, it was requested by the government in Sarajevo to check out those documents. And when I did my expertise, I was not able to know at the time whether this would be contested. I didn't think that there would be any trouble in checking out the documents. My report -- the findings in my report were based on the documents of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica, number 657-8-1/93, dated the 8th of June, 1993. It is the situation report on the free territory of the staff of the supreme command and sent to Sarajevo personally to Sefer Halilovic. Second, the republican staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina, OS Srebrenica number 35/93, dated the 30th of August, 1993, a list of fighters and, in inverted commas, the Naser Unit to the command to the 2nd Corps in Tuzla. Third, the staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica, the number of the document was 35/93; its date, the 30th of August, 1993; and it was a list of the communication service attached to Srebrenica of the 2nd Corps of Tuzla. The fourth was the staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica, the wartime presidency. The number of that document was 664/93, and the date was the 19th of August, 1993, and its title was "A review of the formation and establishment of --"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, General, General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to tell you the documents or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's not necessary for you to give lists and lists and lists of documents. You're an expert. You have come here. You have told this Court that you have assessed all of the material that has been made available to you. On the basis of that material, what is the correct figure; an approximate figure, but what is the correct approximate figure for the number of Muslim fighters that were in the Srebrenica enclave in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct figure of the Muslim fighters in Srebrenica was, according to the documents that I wanted to read out to the end when you interrupted me - I don't know why, it was for you to be able to check them out - it was 10.913 fighters on the basis of the documents which the Muslim army from Srebrenica sent to its superior commands. I was -- and I was more apt to accept that figure because -- and that is why I wrote it down in my report because I assumed that that type of document would be a surer figure, more reliable; whereas the intelligence data that the VRS arrived at, or any other army for that matter, would not have that degree of reliability because this was done on the basis of assessments on what the prisoners of war said, perhaps, or other people in the service of the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your report is incorrect, isn't it, General? The written report is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I kindly request that you take care that the report is based on documentation or assessment. This is based on documentation. And in my oral testimony, I bore in mind the fact that there were indices, pointers, to the fact that parts of the forces from Srebrenica were sent to the operation around Sarajevo in the spring of 1995. And we have testimony about that in the book by Sefer Halilovic who was at one time the Commander-in-Chief of the VRS and of the BiH, and I thought that this fact should be taken into account and that the number 10.913, to that number should be added the police forces, and that this should be reduced to the number that I quote here which I think is more realistic than the figure mentioned in the Muslim documents that were sent to the superior commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have Defence Exhibit 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, which is the realistic figure? You've given the Judges three different figures: The figure in your report; the figure that you provided to Mr. Visnjic, which was 8 to 10.000; and then the figure that you've just given to me in cross-examination, which is 5 to 6.000 and is, in fact, based on this VRS intelligence report. Which is the most realistic figure, in your view? Just give me the numbers, General; I don't want any explanation. Just in your expert opinion, which is the most reliable figure?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to provide a precise answer to your question, and that is why during the examination-in-chief I only gave an assessment of that figure and not a figure which can be based on documents. I could not be precise as regards the total number because I don't know how many soldiers left for the Sarajevo operation from the Srebrenica enclave. It could have been 1.000, 2.000, but it could have been also more. And that is the reason why I gave you the number which was given by the intelligence service of the VRS, and also the number which was given by the BiH army, and also my assessment as to what it would be logical to expect concerning the men under arms in Srebrenica. That is the reason why the number that I gave to this Chamber is an assessment reached on the basis of the situation and the number of soldiers who were registered, and also on the basis of the number of the soldiers which were seconded for the Sarajevo operation, and on the basis of information which was given by Sefer Halilovic in his book, "The Cannon Strategy." So that is an overall analysis on the basis of which I gave you the figure 7 to 8.000 soldiers in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, if you look at this report in front of you, and I'm summarising it - this is a VRS report which I assume you must have seen last night which is why you've changed the figures - you'll see this is a VRS report of June 24th from the Milici Brigade. It states that there were 5.000, 5.000 armed soldiers, 550 soldiers from the East Bosnian Battalion, and then I think -- sorry, from the manoeuvring task force, and 350 soldiers from the East Bosnia Light Infantry Battalion, of which 3.000 it states were armed, mainly with local and foreign-made small arms. Now, you would agree with me that when one places this piece of evidence against your report, which states that there were 13.000 armed people in Srebrenica, and your evidence to Mr. Visnjic, that your evidence is in fact a gross exaggeration of the reality on the ground at the time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The number of soldiers that I gave was calculated on the basis of the Muslim documentation, and it was my assumption that they had no reasons to lie to their superior command, but that they had an accurate insight into the actual number of soldiers. As to the information provided by the Commander of the Milici Brigade, in the first paragraph of his order concerning intelligence data about the enemy, something that I cannot consider reliable enough, I think that the information that is given by a subordinate command to its -- to superior command is far more reliable. This is something that is done on the basis of records, on the basis of relevant information books, and on the basis of the situation in the relevant territory. That is on the basis of the factual situation on the ground. So from that number, I deducted the assessed number of men who could have been in Sarajevo. That is, the people who were not in the enclave at that time. And the number I reached was 7.000 to 8.000, and I believe that that figure is more correct than the one given by the Milici Brigade, regardless of the fact that they gave their information in a document signed by A Captain who was a captain first class at the time, and did he not have adequate information. He did not have an opportunity to assess correctly the number of the soldiers in the enclave. And my assessment was given on the relevant reports sent by the Muslim side to their superior commands either in Tuzla or in Sarajevo. So that is the reason, sir, why there is variance here between numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, while we still see this page on the screen, I have to say that General Radinovic said in response to my answer that the number was between 8.000 and 10.000 and not between 6.000 and 7.000, as far as I can recall. And not 13.000. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What line are you talking about, Mr. Visnjic? We have a number of figures here on the screen. What is the number of the line that you wish to correct? Has it disappeared already?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can actually correct the situation for my learned friend. In his evidence to Mr. Visnjic, the witness said 8.000 to 10.000 men. In his report, he says, I think, 10.000 to 13.000 men. He's now saying 5.500 to 6.000 men. You can check the report if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's on page 14, line 24. The error was in the question put by my learned colleague Mr. Cayley. That is why I wanted to react, but it's gone. It's no longer on the screen. I just wanted to correct the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the transcript speaks for itself. I remember that General Radinovic said in response to your question 10.000 or 8.000. That was the answer that I remember as being given by General Radinovic. I hope that the record is clear. Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you stated in your evidence to Mr. Visnjic that two and a half battalions of the Drina Corps took part in operation Krivaja 95. Could you please give me a proximate figure for the number of men from the Bosnian Serb army who would have been engaged within those two and a half battalions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were two and a half battalions that took active part in the first echelon of the attack, but the Bratunac Brigade troops and the Milici Brigade troops were in contact with the enemy. There was one company of the Vlasenica Brigade and the Skelani Battalion. So if I remember it correctly, and I think I do, I said that this would be the equivalent of a brigade. Objectively speaking, in the first echelon of the attack there were only two brigades that -- two battalions that -- two and a half battalions that took part - that was the combat group from the Zvornik Brigade - and also units from the 2nd Motorised Brigade and the Birac brigade. So that was the first echelon of the attack, that is two and a half battalions together with a company which was on the left wing. At the same time, north, east, and west there were forces of the Birac Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade -- Bratunac and Milici Brigade. We can speak of a brigade relatively reduced in size which took place -- took part in the activities around Srebrenica, and that is why I said that the ratio of forces between the VRS and the forces inside the Srebrenica enclave was, according to my calculation, 1. -- 1 to 2.8 to the advantage of the 28th Division. But it could have been even more disadvantageous. However, if we calculate the ratio of forces, the criterion is that a mistake must not be made in the affirmative, in the positive way. One should not exaggerate by giving the advantage to the enemy because the attacker has to have advantage in order to ensure success.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, how many men approximately, how many men approximately were there in that light VRS brigade? Do we just take 5.500 and divide by 2.8? Is that how we get to the figure?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So how many men? General, you're an expert. You're a lieutenant general. You know how many men are in these. Give me a figure. One, two, three? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately there were between 1.500 to 2.000 active participants in the action, that is, the soldiers who were taking active part in combat. However, as regards the overall control of the enclave, there were many more, of course. There were the forces of the Milici Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade. But when you calculate the ratio of forces, you have to calculate the troops who are in contact with the enemy, not those who are not taking active part in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if we include not just the active participants but, of course, as you say, all of those who were, to quote you -- there were many more, you said. There were many more. "However, as regards overall control of the enclave, there were many more." What was the total figure? Two thousand plus what, General? Give me an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not calculate that ratio of forces because it was not essential for my analysis. It would have been necessary for me to make a new calculation and to take into account what were the forces which could have exerted a certain amount of influence. What I calculated was the ratio of forces engaged in the attack, who participated in active combat, and that was the ratio of forces that I came up with. If you want me to make a calculation for something else, then you have to give me some additional time to do that. I need some time to make an appropriate calculation if you want me to speak about another context. I don't want to play with figures here. I don't think you do either. I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not -- General, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- just present you with figures off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what I'm asking you for is a total approximate figure of the VRS forces engaged in the attack on the Srebrenica enclave. I don't want you to give me to the last man, but an approximate figure. You're the expert. You're a General. You tell me what it was from the documents that you've seen. If you can't tell the Court, then just say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the documents concerning combat activities in and around Srebrenica, less than 2.000 members of the VRS took part in that operation, in those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So less than 2.000. And based on the Milici Brigade document that --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- we've just seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an objection which might be helpful for my learned colleague and his questions. The General said that on the basis of the documents concerning active combat activities. This word "active" is left out from the interpretation and that is likely to cause problems. What we're talking about here are active combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, so based on the Milici Brigade document which you actually quoted the figure earlier and then subsequently said it was unreliable, which states the VRS themselves state that there were about 3.000 armed men in the enclave, if you compare the 2.000 members of the VRS against the 3.000 armed Muslims in the enclave, the ratio is nothing like 2.8 to 1 in favour of the Muslims, is it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure that you have in the document about armed Muslims is not correct. If you consider the relevancy of the document, this is an order issued by the Commander of the Milici Brigade, that is, one of the commanding officers of a tactical unit within the Drina Corps, and this particular data is not accurate. The number of men under weapons in the enclave, that is, the number of troops of the 28th Division, exceeds by far the figure given here, and I can give you the exact figure as to how many men were under arms. I can also be specific in terms of the kind of weapons that they had. According to Muslim sources, I have the relevant information, including the type of weapons that they had in the Srebrenica enclave, and I thought that for the purposes of assessing the strengths of the Tactical Group that it was enough to have in mind the overall situation and the tactical context so that we can get an accurate picture of everything else that followed from that fact and what is the subject matter of these proceedings. I didn't expect an expert military discussion about tactical issues. Of course, I am ready to engage in such a discussion, of course, but you will have to provide me with the relevant information. The number was higher than 3.000, and the figure that you have in this document is absolutely not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, for your information, the Judges have heard evidence from the second-in-command of the Dutch Battalion who was inside the enclave, and he estimated the number of troops, the number of Muslim fighters, at a maximum of 4.500 soldiers. Were you in the Srebrenica enclave in July of 1995, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I studied the documents which were issued by the Muslim commanders to their superiors, and those figures are more correct than the ones estimated by the Dutch Battalion. Muslim officers were trying to conceal the information regarding the number of soldiers and the type of weapons from the Dutch because, according to the agreement, they were supposed to hand over those weapons, which they didn't do. And this is common knowledge to everybody, including the commander of the Dutch Battalion at the time and other relevant factors within the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in giving the figures of Muslim troops in the enclave, you've relied exclusively on Muslim documentation and have ignored all other documentary and oral testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You are interpreting my words erroneously. That was not my intention. You're trying to put to me things that I didn't say. I said that I based myself on a number of sources, and that I took into account the most reliable sources. The most reliable piece of information for myself is the one which was given by the Muslim commander to his superior command in Tuzla and Sarajevo because I think that he was not in a position to lie to them. Everything else is far less reliable. So those information is the most reliable one. Mobilisational reports, operational reports, reports on morale sent by the command of the 28th Division, a former 8th Operative Group, and before that the staff for Srebrenica, so that kind of documentation was the most reliable for me. That was the most reliable source, and it was on the basis of those sources that I reached my conclusions concerning the number of soldiers. But I also took into account the information -- this information here, these figures here, the ones that you mentioned, but I thought them to be far less reliable than the sources of the Muslim army which sent relevant reports to its superiors about those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is the figure of 12 to 13.000 combatants quoted in paragraph 2.9 of your report, is that a reliable figure?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of information contained in these documents, it is a reliable figure; however, from that figure I deducted the number of the soldiers who might have been in the Sarajevo theatre of operations participating in the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo. So the figure has to be corrected; a deduction must be made. I'm not sure about that number of soldiers, but that was my assessment, so that the overall figure for Srebrenica would be approximately 8.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on, General, and let's talk about Operation Krivaja 95 itself. Now, you said in your evidence that the main feature that had to be taken by VRS forces moving into the enclave was the Alibegovac feature, and you said that the route of advance for that particular objective was on the route of advance of the Romanija Brigade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the 2nd Battalion, the 2nd Combat Group which took that route. Basically, yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you turn to page 31 of your report, and if you could read out the -- this is paragraph 4.3, and it's at the top of page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Usher, it's page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you have page 31 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you read the first sentence of paragraph 4.3, please, General? Paragraph 4.3, the first sentence, please, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I should like to ask, unless that is contrary to the procedure here -- I have been testifying for 5 days already, and I have serious problems with my throat. Could you perhaps read it out and it can be recorded in the transcript, and I will answer your question, if that is at all possible? If I were not 61 years old, I would have long exhausted my powers of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can do that, General. "Engaged forces from the Birac and 2nd Romanija Brigade encountered unexpectedly strong resistance on their routes of advance and they were late in carrying out their immediate task."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Both of those witnesses testified to this court that there was essentially little or no resistance on their lines of advance, and I will just very briefly read to you what they said. Private Borovcanin, who was in the forward reconnaissance unit, said the following in answer to my learned friend Mr. Petrusic: "So my question was --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Q. So my question was, when you reached this position at Alibegovac, it was no serious conflict with your unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No." Same witness said: "Q. On the way to Kiprovo or, rather, Alibegovac, did you encounter any resistance by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had some minor resistance at Kiprovo."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Q. In the course of these combat operations, did you in fact comply with the order, act on it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did because, that is to say, we had a direction of movement. There was no resistance from Muslim forces, so that we took control of that feature easily." Now, you would agree with me, General, that two eyewitnesses, two members of the VRS actually engaged in the operation to take Srebrenica, would have a more accurate recollection than the opinion that you give here? You'd agree with me that when you say that there was unexpectedly strong resistance, it's completely incorrect, isn't it, based on the testimony of those two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it is not a question, it is your assessment of my expert report. That is your right. It is your right to make those assessments, and it is up to the -- Their Honours to assess what is correct with respect to truth and what is correct with respect to conduct. If the time from the line of development, that is to say, when the operation was launched on the 6th up until the entry into Srebrenica, and especially up until they reached the line of the assignment itself which was ordered in the order for active combat activities, if four days went by and such a small depth of territory, then I don't understand why such a short space of time took so long to pass if there was over -- if there was no resistance. I personally feel that when an army moves into the attack, it wants to arrive at the line of the assignment as soon as possible which was defined in the order in spacial terms. This particular brigade, that combat group made up of the units from those two brigades, was rather late, lagged behind, rather. And from the documents that I studied for this purpose, I did not -- unfortunately, I wrote my report before those witnesses testified here, so I did not study those testimonies. But to tell you the truth, the witness who saw that might have gained that impression; however, the fact remains that these forces reached the -- their line of their assignment only on the 10th. Why? Well, I think it was because of the resistance that was offered by the defenders; otherwise, they would have reached that line and that assignment the first day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General, of course this is an inference. This is your inference, which is logical, but could it happen that they took some time not to appear in the eyes of the world that there is an invasion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I can't enter into that type of speculation, Your Honour, because it runs contrary to my logics, and my mental composition is that of a soldier so I can't enter into that form of speculation. That is not my realm of endeavour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could prepare Prosecutor's Exhibit 428.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you stated in your evidence that it was obvious to you that the corps artillery did not take part in these activities in operation Krivaja 95. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To be quite precise, the corps artillery group and not the corps artillery. There was corps artillery. It was the corps artillery group. Although in the order for the corps artillery group there is that position, but as far as I know, it was not active.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could turn, Mr. Usher, to page 3. I'll summarise the document, Mr. President, because I have a lot to refer to. But it's at the bottom of page 5, Mr. Usher. The bottom of page 5, the page that you have. Page 3. I'm sorry. Page 3, going on to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you, General, paragraph 5 which is on your page 2? I will summarise the document as we go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, is the Krivaja 95 document, the order of General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "5. Tasks of the units for separating and reducing the enclaves in size." It then gives a task to the 1st Battalion and it states that the 1st Battalion, on the next page - if you go to the next page, Mr. Usher, at the top - is to be supported by the corps artillery group. If we then go down to the 2nd Battalion and its tasks, we see -- and, Mr. Usher, if you could move that up. Again we see to be supported by KAG, the corps artillery group, as per plan and request. If we then turn the page and we go to the next section which deals with the Bratunac Light -- the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade forces, at the top, again, we see, at the top of the TV screen, to be supported by KAG corps artillery group, as per plan and request. If we go to the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade, we see to be supported by corps artillery group, as per plan and request. Then - if you can move that page up, please, Mr. Usher - in the launching of the attack -- and this is the general instruction just above the artillery support section. In the launching of the attack, the forces in direct contact to be supported by the artillery and by the corps artillery group as per plan and request command post in the area of Pribicevac. Then to summarise, in paragraph 6, it talks about the composition of the corps artillery group, basic firing position in the area of Pribicevac, tasks during preparatory fire, to neutralise entry targets as per plan for preparatory fire. Duration of preparatory fire, supporting fire for the attack as per plan and request with emphasis on the first and second axes of advance. Now, General, you would certainly agree with me that General Zivanovic believed that the corps artillery group was, in fact, engaged in the attack on Srebrenica in Krivaja 95, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, no, for the simple reason - you don't have to know this, it's not your profession to - but when orders are issued, they are issued to units. The corps artillery group is formed by its artillery platoon, mixed -- regiment, I'm sorry, regiment, the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment. Had that Mixed Artillery Regiment had to be active, it would have been stipulated here explicitly. The Commander of the regiment would have stated that he was forming a corps artillery group, and a corps artillery group is formed from the Mixed Artillery Regiment, and parts of the Mixed Artillery Regiment are attached to brigades where the activity is greatest for them to be able to form their brigade artillery groups. There was no need whatsoever for the corps artillery group to go into action because it was not an attack operation by the corps but, rather, it was an operation for active combat activities of a tactical level, and in that type of endeavour, the corps artillery does not make part. In part 4 which you read out -- I'm sorry, point 6 on page 4 of the document, point 6 that you read out, it says fire support and then -- that is artillery support, then underneath that we have the KAG, the corps artillery group and its composition, and it does not state in that point which units of the mixed artillery regiment, what calibre of that regiment, that is to say, what type of artillery makes up the corps artillery group. Furthermore, in the plan of the operation itself, Krivaja, we do not have the plan for the action of the artillery which is an indispensable plan for any kind of artillery fire to be realised within -- as support to the forces engaged in the operation. As I did not find in the documents for the operation Krivaja 95 a plan for the activities of the artillery which include artillery fire that is to be realised in preparation for the attack and in support for the attack and when and according to what signal, following what signal in time and space and in the context of the dynamics at which the forces are engaged fire is transferred from one position to another. Therefore, not to have any firing or firepower on one's own -- one's own form, the dynamics of fire is very strictly planned and there is a set mechanism in which this is implemented and transferred. As I did not find this and the commander in point 6 did not stipulate the composition of that artillery group, then my logical assumption was that that group did not -- was not, in fact, active at all, did not engage in action. And for me to be able to draw that conclusion, and this need not be relevant for this Trial Chamber, I also arrived at that conclusion from a conversation during the preparation of my expert report when numerous officers from different command levels in the army of Republika Srpska, including some members the Command of the Drina Corps as well as some members of the Command of the Main Staff. And each one of those people to whom I talked said that the corps artillery was not used. And when I looked at the filming of the entry of the Republika Srpska into Srebrenica, as there was no -- at least, I was not able to see no great destruction and devastation, for me that was a sign that the high calibres of the type of howitzers, 155-millimetres, were not used because the effects and consequences have been far graver.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, just one moment, please. Perhaps this would be an opportune moment to take a break, because I see that General Radinovic has been speaking for eight minutes continuously, and I think he will need to rest his throat, his voice. Also, General Radinovic, I should like to profit from the occasion to ask you to be more direct in your answers to questions. I do understand that you know many things and that you have a need to express them here, but if you try to go straight to the heart of the question, answering the question directly, you will benefit and so will your throat. So I think that you could perhaps try to do this. You said that you were having a throat problem, a problem with your voice. So let's take a 20-minute break. And for everybody to be able to plan ahead, we will be resuming at five minutes past twelve and go on until ten minutes past one. At ten minutes past one, we will have our 40-minute break for lunch. So that is how we shall proceed. But let's take a 20-minute break now, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. Please proceed. General, have you had a rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could Prosecutor's Exhibit 425 be placed on the ELMO, and I think the General already has that document in front of him. And do we already have 428 on the ELMO? Yes. Keep that one to hand, 425; 428, if you leave on the ELMO. I'm sorry, 428 on the ELMO, and keep 425 in your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you have the first page of Prosecutor's Exhibit 425 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no. 425, yes, 425 I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, this is the Krivaja 95 order from Zivanovic, the one that we've just been referring to before the break which contained all the references to the corps artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I'm going to read, in order to save your voice, and I'm just going to read out where the order expresses, "To the commands of," and then it refers to all of the infantry brigades involved in the operation, and then lastly it refers to the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment, the very unit that you stated would have had to have received this order in order for a corps artillery group to be put together for this. Now, General, you would agree with me that General Zivanovic would not have sent this order to the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment if he had not intended a corps artillery group to be formed, would he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with you only in part. Had he had the intention to form it, he would have formed it and gave it, assigned it, fire positions, reserve fire positions, and follow-up fire positions. And he would have stated its composition, that is to say, he would have ordered directly to the commander of the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment to form a corps artillery group of the following composition, with the divisions and artillery pieces and everything else that the group would require; and on the basis of that, the chief of artillery would have devised and drew up a plan for its action for preparation and for support. As I did not come across those documents, and they are the sole documents on the basis of which artillery fire can be opened as a planned action, so as I did not come across that in the documents that were made available to me, I concluded that that plan of action was never compiled; and on the basis of that, I concluded that the corps artillery group was, in fact, not engaged at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the order, orders are -- also include things that are not realised, not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're going to have to trim down your answers because otherwise we're going to be here for a very, very long time during this cross-examination. So what I would like you to do is to answer my questions directly when I put a direct question to you. I don't expect you to answer yes or no, you can give an explanation, but you don't need to give, as the President pointed out earlier, an eight-minute answer to a question that probably took about 10 seconds to ask you. I'm not insisting that you say yes or no; you can give an explanation, but a brief explanation. Now, General, I'll read out a section of this order. In paragraph 6, where General Zivanovic is speaking about artillery support, he states, "During preparatory fire to neutralise the enemy targets as per plan for preparatory fire." Now, General Zivanovic is referring, isn't he, to an artillery plan, paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's on page 5, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you can see at the bottom of the TV screen, General, it says, "During preparatory fire to neutralise the enemy targets as per plan for preparatory fire." Now, General, you would agree with me that when General Zivanovic signed this order, he anticipated that there would be a plan for preparatory fire, even if you haven't seen it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask you to read point 7, the following point immediately after point 6? Could you read that point out, please, point 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Anti-tank combat."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "In all units of company and battalion size, form an anti-tank group and have it in readiness for combat against the enemy armoured forces." Now, General, answer my question first of all, and I'll repeat it, General. I'll repeat it to you, General. Would you agree with me that when General Zivanovic signed this order, he anticipated that there would be a plan for preparatory fire, even if you haven't actually seen that order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In point 7, he stipulates the anti-tank combat although he knew the Muslim forces in Srebrenica no possibility whatsoever to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, please, I'm going to start insisting because now I'm getting far behind in my cross-examination. The witness is going to be here a very long time. I insist that he answers the question or declines to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. And we too are going to be lagging behind. General, could you please go directly to the question. If you don't agree, say you don't agree; or if you don't know, say you don't know, but please give us a direct answer, otherwise, we'll be going round and round in circles.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am answering in the best way possible, as I deem fit for the question, and I have tried to indicate to Mr. Cayley, the distinguished Prosecutor, that the orders contain many things which are written down but never implemented in practice, and if we wish to get to the end of the proceedings, we have to go back to basics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, General. The question that you were asked was at the level of not realisation but what was provided for forecast, and what the Prosecutor asked you was that he -- actually, he wanted to know whether this was forecast, envisaged, not if it was actually implemented and existed. So without further ado, I'm going to give the floor back to Mr. Cayley to ask the question again and to have your direct answer, if possible, please, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I will repeat the question for you. Would you agree with me that when General Zivanovic signed this order, he anticipated that there would be a plan for preparatory fire, even if you have not seen that plan, by the language in paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he does not anticipate a plan. He approves a plan once a plan has been compiled, but artillery fire was not planned nor the corps artillery went into effect. So my only conclusion, and that is the sole one I insist upon, is that the corps artillery group at Srebrenica was not active. We can spend a whole day discussing that, but it is my belief that the corps artillery group was not active and I have sufficient arguments to bear that out. No plan of activity was found and a corps artillery group does not step into action without a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move, please, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 77/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Mr. Cayley. I am going to insist upon this point. Now, at least in paragraph 6 was General Zivanovic mentioning -- did he make mention of a plan in para 6? Does General Zivanovic mention a plan?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentions -- he says "as per plan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I'm going to go through -- I didn't intend doing this, but because of the progress that we're making, I have a whole series of UN military observers' reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 77/1. The General won't be able to read them because they're in English and I don't intend reading all of them, I just intend reading some extracts. If 77/1 could be placed on the ELMO, please. Yes. That's perfect. Mr. Usher, if you could move that document up. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're aware that there were a team of UN military observers within the Srebrenica enclave and indeed you have referred to these UNMO reports in your evidence-in-chief to the Defence, and I think you stated in your evidence-in-chief that these reports were unreliable because they relied on Muslim information. What I will state to you from the outset is that, in fact, these reports flag up whenever information was received from the Muslims, and the UNMOs always stated in these reports that where the information had been received from Muslim forces it was not confirmed because of the concern that they had about reliability, and we'll see that in these reports as we go through them. Let me read to you what happened or what they stated happened on the 6th of July of 1995. "Team Srebrenica reported a Bosnian Serb army offensive launched and ongoing within the enclave as reported under separate cover. The Bosnian Serb army used tanks, artillery, mortars, rockets and heavy machine-gun fire and have targeted the DutchBat headquarters, Bandera Triangle, DutchBat OPs Uniform and Sierra, south of OP Hotel, Potocari township, Srebrenica township. At least 250 artillery and mortar rounds have been recorded so far. The UNMO team have confirmed two fatalities and six casualties so far being taken to hospital." Now, General, you would agree with me that this report indicates that on the 6th of July, the Srebrenica enclave was under an artillery barrage, doesn't it? This was an eyewitness account of what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not claim that the artillery did not act. In my testimony, if I remember correctly, I said that I had information from reports from UN military observers and reports of the Dutch Battalion. Those reports differ with respect to the number of assessed artillery action and their reliability as well. And if I recall, I said that the degree of -- as to the degree of reliability, I consider the reports of the Dutch Battalion to be more relevant because they did this work -- better quality work. Now, when I say that, what do I mean? They recorded explosions. They recorded the explosions and informed of the number of explosions, detonations, and this can be --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, who is firing this artillery? Who is firing the guns into Srebrenica? How did these shells end up in Srebrenica that the UN military observers are recording?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shells did not only end up in Srebrenica, in the urban part, but they also ended up in the positions of the 28th artillery Division around Srebrenica, so that means --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. You're not answering the question. Who was firing the guns?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had those guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And who was that, General? It was the Drina Corps, wasn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Drina Corps and the 28th Division, both. They had guns, too, and mortars. And in the number of identified explosions, there is no data as to the structure of the explosions. They were -- incorporate all the explosions, the 82 millimetre, 120 millimetre, artillery, and gun mortars and shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So what you're saying is the 28th Division was firing from outside of the Srebrenica enclave into the enclave; is that what you're saying? They were actually firing into Srebrenica township and into Potocari, is that -- they had artillery that was firing into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data were not the craters themselves, but just the registered recorded explosions, detonations, not the craters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're not answering my question, and I'm going to keep on interrupting you, until the President stops me, until you answer my question. Are you stating that the 28th Division was firing from outside of the enclave onto their own people? Is that what you're suggesting to the Court?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it the Drina Corps that was firing this artillery into the enclave, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps fired fire positions and defence positions of the 28th Division in order to perform the assignments set by the order for active combat in order to establish military control over the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was the corps artillery group, wasn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the corps artillery group. They were, for the most part, for the most part -- I cannot assess here exactly. For us to know that, we would have to do an on-the-spot examination to examine the craters and the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was running this artillery; which brigades of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally feel that, in the most number of cases, it was the fire groups of the battalions who were within the composition of the forces engaged in active combat, which means fire groups of the battalions mostly. And as testified to by one of the UN observers, he said that they were two shells, 155 millimetres, on the 10th of July. I personally think that they were tank shells and not the 155 millimetre shells because the corps artillery group did not go into action, and a similar impression is left by cannon shells or tank shells. So they registered the detonations, the explosions. They didn't do an on-the-spot examination to ascertain what shell and the type of projectile that was in fact used. So I think that the testimony by the Dutch Battalion is more reliable, although the figures for the shells fired, from the Dutch reports, is greater than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In essence, what you're saying is that the battalions of the Drina Corps who were engaged in Krivaja 95 were the units that were firing the artillery into the enclave; that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that the largest number, and don't keep repeating -- repeat the answers; I have said it. Most of -- when, when the structure of the detonations, the explosions, from the Dutch Battalion report, and I deduced that there were 1.323 over a period of six days. And if we look at the relationship between action and reaction, 1:3, then this means that they were about 1.223 detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can't answer the question, we'll move on to the next report. We're now looking at the 7th of July, "Team Srebrenica reported --"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 77/3, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Team Srebrenica reported that the Bosnian Serb army continued their offensive on the enclave with heavy weapons since early this morning. DutchBat reported heavy shelling around their compound in Potocari and, as a result, three men were injured and brought by Medicins Sans Frontieres to the hospital. UNMOs confirm this. At 1000 hours, unconfirmed reports indicated that the Bosnian Serb army are regrouping around former OP Echo, Company Hill in Bratunac. At 1000 hours, two shells landed in Srebrenica village, but no one was wounded. At 1100 hours, four shells landed in Potocari, no injuries. At 1500 hours, three shells landed in Srebrenica and injured two men. One was picked up by our patrol and another one by Medicins Sans Frontieres, but he died on arrival Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at the hospital. More shells have been landing in the same spot or around, and we suspect that they are from a tank positioned at Company Hill. A lot of damage on buildings has been caused in that area despite the low casualty figures. At 1700 hours, 21 detonations were heard by UNMOs in Potocari. We suspect they are from a multiple-rocket launcher but not confirmed by us. We cannot analyse the craters at the moment due to the continuous shelling but we assess that the Bosnian Serb army are still using mortars, rockets, artillery, and tanks." Now, General, would you agree with me that any informed military officer would conclude based on this UNMO report, whoever received this report in Tuzla, that there was in fact an artillery barrage, a rocket barrage, a mortar barrage being fired into the Srebrenica enclave by Drina Corps units?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not claim, and I repeat that, I did not claim that there was no artillery action. I said that it was not action by the corps artillery group. That is my assertion; that is what I claim. That there was artillery activity, I agree, studying the documents, and artillery activities could have been expected with active combat. How can you have it without fire preparation, preparatory fire? And that was reduced to the battalion fire groups and perhaps some artillery pieces from the artillery of the brigade, but not from the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, just a moment, please. General, in the analysis -- in your analyses of the documents, sources, conversations, and all the elements that helped you to compile your report, you analysed all that material with some criteria in mind, some rules that guided you borne of your experience, borne of your professional training, and borne of your profession proper. Now, I would like to ask you the following: All the rules, all the rules, were they put into practice in the situation that you studied and verified in the documents? Were they all applied? Were they all respected, all these rules and laws? Were they respected?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your question, what I can say is the following: I can give you an answer of principle but not of practice because I was not on the spot for me to be able to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm asking in general terms.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think that they were, yes. According to military doctrine, if inhabited areas were prepared for defence and that military action came from them, then they are legitimate military targets, and I think personally that Mr. Butler confirmed that in his testimony and report as well. He did not contest the legitimacy of the military actions once a decision had been made for that action to be launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was perhaps a little too general. For example, the fact that you didn't see an artillery plan, does that necessarily mean that one -- that the artillery did not exist or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say that the artillery did exist but the corps artillery did not step into action. There was no activity of corps artillery. Mortars, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it did not intervene, but you accept that there was artillery. To whom did that artillery belong, the artillery that did intervene? To whom did it belong?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalions in contact and the brigades in whose zones of responsibility it occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those battalions and those brigades, to which army did they belong?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I'm not going to insist further on, but I hope I will have another opportunity to develop a little bit this question, to know whether the rules were indeed respected in practice. You have told us that not all of the procedures were always applied and respected, but I think we can remain at that for the time being, and I will raise the issue perhaps once again at some other opportunity. Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We'll move on to the 8th of July, General. There are many, many of these reports. I'm not going to go through all of them. I'm going to go through perhaps half a dozen. "8th of July. Shelling started in Srebrenica this morning" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Usher. It's 77/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Shelling started in Srebrenica village this morning at 0800 hours. They seem to be concentrating more on the densely-populated areas," it gives two map references, "and Potocari town. UNMOs have so far counted up to 31 explosions in Potocari but, due to the distance, there may have been more that we have not heard. In Srebrenica town, UNMOs have counted 34 explosions with one landing approximately 20 metres from UNMO accommodation at 1247 hours. Shrapnel was hurled over the PTT building where UNMOs are housed but no one was injured. The Bosnian army Chief of Staff has informed UNMOs that over 100 shells have landed in general area of Biljecevo and Cizmic but this is not confirmed by us. As we are writing this, more shelling is going on in both Potocari and Srebrenica town. We are unable to confirm most of the things even with DutchBat. Unconfirmed information indicates that a hotel located at," it gives a map reference, "has been hit by one shell while two others landed nearby. Any damage or casualties are not known." Then he gives a remark as to the status of this report and that they're heading for the bunkers. Then the update too. "At 1354 hours, DutchBat liaison officer called UNMOs and informed them of their intentions to withdraw from their Observation Post F due to the heavy shelling on their position. They said that their APC will move to a safer place as soon as shelling reduces. UNMO have counted 60 explosions from 1335 hours to 1406 hours. In Srebrenica and Potocari, shelling is still going on. More info to come as we get." Now, General, you would agree by any standards that this is heavy shelling that's going on, isn't it, on the 8th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were just activities for the purposes of demonstration in order for them to reach the features they could control from the enclave. In view of the consequences of the destruction and the structure of the losses and property damage, in view of those consequences, I must say it was really very, very low intensity artillery action. If you bear in mind the geography of the area and how large that area was, and if you compare that with the number of rounds that were fired, from the military point of view, I don't know what it looks like to you, but from my point of view, it is indeed a very low intensity action. But let me say once again that each shell that does not hit the target which is a military target, that hits a civilian target, is a very serious one, of course, but you have to bear in mind the fact that military action was going on in that area, and what happened was - let me use the buzzword - the collateral damage. We always have this problem of conflict of principles, the principle of humanitarian warfare and the principle of military warfare, and those two principles will always be conflicting. I cannot justify a single shell which hit a civilian target, however, it can be expected. But let me assure you that, in view of the standards of military activities in general, this is indeed very low intensity action and very restricted number, very low number of artillery shells and mortars compared to the number of shells which would be fired in a usual military action. If you imagine a clash of two equally strong armies, if you compare that to that situation, you will realise that this was indeed really very low intensity action, although it might be rather cynical for me to say this in this context, but it was indeed very low intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, the Alibegovac feature was the principal first target of the Romanija Brigade, of the 1st Echelon Forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that, General, was in the south of the enclave, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this report, General, indicates that on the 8th of July, all of the highly-populated areas, Potocari in the centre of the enclave, were being shelled. You'd agree with me, General, that the Potocari township and Srebrenica itself are not on the Alibegovac feature, are they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but you will also have to agree with me when I say that military action is not conducted in the way you think it is conducted. You have to put up a certain show of force in order to avoid intervention from the forces from that direction towards the main line of advance, the main line of attack. You have to provide a fire support on certain other lines. Had the forces appeared from the direction of Potocari towards Alibegovac, then the number of losses and the destruction in that area would be far greater. It is now debatable as to what is better, but that is the part of the military doctrine. A commander undertakes tactical activities, tactical steps which are intended to prevent action from the enemy.
