Those are activities for the purposes of show of force which are put up in order to avoid the enemy forces to appear on the main line of attack, and that is how military action is conducted. That is how warfare is being conducted. This is completely in accordance with the principles of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can move now, General, to the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Even if it's full of civilians? You say it's a principle of warfare, even if there is no military activity, to avoid attack of the enemy. Even if civilians are there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is not what I said. I said that what we commonly refer to as collateral damage is something that is, unfortunately, unavoidable in any war. So when targeting a military target, or an assumed military target, an erroneous assessment can be made. There are unfortunate incidents of targeting hospitals. NATO probably didn't wish to target hospitals in Belgrade, but it did hit them. But that's war. That's how things happen. Or perhaps the settlement in Aleksinac or that train which happened to be on the bridge which was targeted. I'm perfectly sure it was not the intention of the NATO to shell those targets and that intention cannot be imputed to them, but that is a kind of risk is understood, which is implied in any war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I think you said in your evidence to Mr. Visnjic that the operation to take the Srebrenica enclave essentially was completed on the night of the 9th of July, morning of the 10th of July; is that right? The Alibegovac feature was taken at that point in time, from your assessment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been an error in interpretation. I didn't say that the operation of the takeover of Srebrenica was completed but that the operation of the accomplishment of assignments of the Krivaja 95 operation, that is, the taking control of military features for the purposes of deactivating and neutralising, militarily speaking, the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was completed by the night of the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 9th or -- I don't have a precise piece of information, but my estimate is that it took place sometime in the evening hours of the 9th, but that perhaps is a date -- is information that could be contested, but I will take that risk. My assessment is that it took place in the evening of the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me read to you the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is 77/12, Mr. Usher. We can put that on the ELMO. This is the UNMO report from that day, from the 10th of July. "Shelling is still going on in Srebrenica. Up till now, we UNMOs confirm from the morning over 100 detonations. 0930 about eight rockets were fired from," and then it gives a grid reference, "in the direction of Srebrenica. Then at 1255 on the 10th of July, two heavy shells, probably 155-millimetre shells, hit the direct surroundings of the hospital at 1100 hours. All the windows are smashed and shrapnel has showered the rooms and walls of the hospital. The surgery is very difficult to proceed. The number of casualties and wounded we don't know yet, but we will inform you as soon as possible. It looks as if the Bosnian Serb army are now targeting the hospital and the surroundings." And then a further report, and this is 77/14, Mr. Usher. Mr. Usher, don't worry, we'll leave that one. Don't worry about 77/14, I'll ask it on this one. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, based on your theory of events that by the evening of the 9th of July the enclave had been deactivated and neutralised, militarily speaking, why would the Drina Corps shell the hospital if by that time, by the 10th of July, in your evidence, the enclave had been deactivated?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't answer your question because I'm not familiar with the context in which it took place. It is possible that the target was something else and that it was missed, whoever was operating the artillery piece. It is possible for a very precise projectile to miss the target, let alone an artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very highly probable for such a thing to occur in any war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, in your own words, you stated that by the evening of the 9th of July, the enclave had been neutralised; it had been deactivated from a military point of view. Why did the Bosnian Serb army shell the hospital in Srebrenica on the 10th if there was no longer a military threat?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was probably some kind of counter-attack from Srebrenica because, as you know, the 28th Division gathered in the area of Susnjari and Jaglici on the 11th. Up until then, its brigades and parts of its brigades were still probably somewhere in the area. Their movement was observed, and I'm sure that there was need to continue action towards certain resistance points which were still active at the time. I didn't say that the enclave was captured; I said that conditions were created for its deactivation and for the takeover of the dominant hills around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 30, paragraph 283 of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is the Secretary-General's report, General, 10th of July. "The Bosnian Serb army continued to shell the town throughout the day. B Company also reported a number of fire fights between the Bosnian army and the Bosnian Serb army at various locations. UNHCR reported that an estimated 2.000 civilians had begun to gather around the hospital, hoping that its special status might protect them from Serb fire. UNHCR also reported that by approximately 1300 hours, six civilians had been killed and 23 wounded as a result of the shelling. Between around 1100 hours and 1800 hours, however, the Bosnian Serb army did not fire directly at UNPROFOR blocking positions." General, there were 2.000 civilians gathered around the hospital, and the Bosnian Serb army opened fire with heavy artillery on that hospital. Do you think that was an accident?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was an accident. Were there any fatalities in that action? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Six civilians killed, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was saying to you all the time, and after all, that is the subject of this report, was that the activities were still ongoing and that it could only be expected for such activities to take place until -- up until such a time as the enemy forces are still active.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, on the 11th of July, 5.000 civilians were gathered in the town of Srebrenica around Bravo Company, around the UN compound. 5.000 civilians. And this report indicates that, on that day at around 1330 hours, the Bosnian Serb army fired two shells which impacted in B Company compound where 4 to 5.000 Bosniak civilians were taking refuge. An unspecified number were injured. Were you aware that this event took place, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this in the Secretary-General's report, and I do not have any reasons not to believe that. However, those are consequences of war activities which take place everywhere, which took place everywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, anywhere in the world. In Yugoslavia, we had 2.500 killed civilians and 400 killed soldiers, so many more civilians than soldiers, and civilians were not the target of the military action. That's what happens in any war. This is not something that I can justify, but you have to understand that it is a perfectly normal consequence of a war. War is also a misfortune, and it is always the greatest misfortune for the civilians who always suffer most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, the reason that the Bosnian Serb army went on shelling is because they wanted to frighten the population, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're not asking me questions, you're putting things to me. I cannot agree with you, no, because that was not the objective of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, do you recall in your evidence that you said that none of the UN protection force positions were the object of attack? Do you recall that in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was speaking in principle. I said that the UN was not the target, was not the objective of the attack; and that was indeed contained in the orders of the VRS, that is, that the UN forces should not constitute targets for them. However, they happened to be in the same enclave where the Muslim forces were, so the risk was there for them to become endangered during those activities that were taking place against the members of the 28th Division. It's one and the same area. They were not located somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But to your knowledge, was the UN compound which was shelled, was it close to any military target, any military which -- where the Muslim army was, 28th Division was, to your knowledge? Was it close by? Or usually the official UN compound was rather isolated.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a specific answer for specific checkpoints, but the Muslim positions were immediately behind the lines which were held by the Dutch Battalion. As to specific checkpoints, I don't know, but I know that a certain amount of military cunningness is necessary. It would have been perfectly normal for the 28th Division to have parts of its force deployed around UNPROFOR positions because those were the most protected points, and it was only to be expected that those would be the places of the lowest intensity. As far as I know, UNPROFOR checkpoints were not the target. As to whether they were exposed to a certain amount of danger during the activities that were being conducted against the Muslim forces, that, to me, again, constitutes a very likeable consequence of -- a very likely consequence of the tactics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is there any indication that the UN, the UN compound served as shelter for the Muslim forces, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, I have a piece of information, and I consider it to be reliable, that in the post office building, in the basement, was the centre of communications of the 28th Division; and so towards that feature there was probably action on the part of the VRS. It probably did. But now, whether it was a post -- in a post office or in another feature, that is negligible for a general assessment, but I just quote it as information, as an example. In an inhabited area, military targets cannot be completely outside and divorced from civilian facilities. And of course, the civilian features and facilities also are in jeopardy, and this -- and there I include the UN, as well, forces. And the worst thing is the unprotected civilians. That is the worst consequence of wars of this type waged on a small area where the parties are mixed; the fronts are mixed, they are taken control over by one side and then another, and that is the whole unfortunate characteristic of small wars and wars of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, let's go straight back to what His Honour Judge Riad was speaking about. The Judges have heard evidence from many of the Dutch personnel who were in the enclave at the time, and Major Franken, who was the Deputy Commander, was asked questions by myself about the shelling that took place on the 10th and 11th of July, and he said the following. This is my question: "Q. You said at the beginning of the answer to my question that you heard reports of pretty massive shelling of the city, and you also said that at that time, to your knowledge, the 28th Division had vanished, had disappeared?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why was there --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down for the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "Q. Why was there shelling of the city taking place?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's strange you ask me that question, but there was not any military objective other than the so-called telegraph post and telegraph building where a part of the headquarters of the 28th Division was. But that was not in the city, that was in the northern part of the city. The city itself did not give any military objective in that stage, other than, of course, the UN forces. But then again, it was at random shooting at the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From your recollection, what was the calibre of the artillery and mortars? And if you can remember to pause between my question and answer, I'll try to go more slowly myself.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly it was bigger calibres of around --" And then the transcript is not clear. "I did deduce from that the explosions we heard and we saw, so it was heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Any other weapons being used, Major Franken, apart from heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tanks were used, not only on the positions of our own forces, but also used to shoot into area of the city." The witness then states, and I won't read all of it, that B Company counted 200 shells. I finally asked him: "Q. Now, you stated in an earlier response that there was no military objective by this stage that would require this level of firing, and I'll ask you the question again. In your opinion, what was the reason for this very heavy shelling?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could have been two reasons, but it was the same effect: killing people, or trying to raise a panic by killing people. And I mean by `people' civilians, women and children." Now, General, you have already stated that you regard the Dutch evidence as reliable information, and you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that a man, a professional army officer of 30 years' experience on the ground in the enclave at the time, would have a better idea than you about the reason for the continuous artillery shelling on the 10th and 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the reason -- that it was more jeopardised and that he was on the spot, yes; but as to the reason, I cannot support you in your opinion there that he knew that better than me. I can know better what the reason was. Whether the VRS -- or rather, those who opened fire, whether they knew where the 28th Division was located on the 10th and 11th, they did not know. And up until the time that all contact was -- that you lose all contact with the enemy, you continue your actions until all contact with the enemy is lost. And I'm quite sure that nobody from the command system in the army of Republika Srpska ordered for any targets, for any reasons whatsoever, that fire be opened on a concentration of civilians. I cannot accept that because it goes contrary to the ethics of warfare, which is something that I have striven for all my life, and I'm quite certain that the army of Republika Srpska did not do that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I apologise for interrupting, I would like to ask something now. Why do you say that no officer would have ordered that? Why do you say that? What is the basis for your assertion? Because it's the rule, is that all? Because it's the rule or do you have any special information in that regard?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it is the rule, yes. And everybody is trained to apply that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You spoke of ethics, General. So for military rules, for military honour, to say that no officer would have ordered that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, I also had numerous interviews with people who took part in the operation, and I asked them precisely about that problem. In asking them about that, my answer was that nobody had done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General. You said the officers of the VRS. Now, having seen everything that you have seen and read, are you convinced that there were executions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there were executions. Not on the part of the leaders and commanders of army of Republika Srpska, officers that command the battalions, brigades, and corps. Unfortunately, I do know that there were executions, but that was not done by the system of command of the Drina Corps. They were not responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that no officer of the VRS did so. Now I'm asking you the question why, if you admit that there were executions, why is that principle valid for the questions of executions, that is, that no officer could have done anything like that? You say that on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who did it. I can't answer that question. I consider that the officers of the army of Republika Srpska were not allowed to do so and did not do so, but who did do so, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That means that in your opinion, the executions were implemented by somebody who was -- who could never have belonged to the VRS. Is that what you're telling us? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps they did belong to the VRS. Perhaps they did or perhaps there were some other forces which were not in the composition and under the control of the Drina Corps. We're talking about the responsibility of the Drina Corps, the accountability of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we -- we're not going to continue. It is ten minutes past one, and I think the time has come to take a lunch break. I see in the transcript that I said 50 minutes for the break. I said 40 minutes, but as I see 50 in the transcript and people might have a programme of their own, I shall abide by what the transcript says and not by what I said. Perhaps the interpreters made a slight correction there which was more convenient to them, but anyway, no problem there. I said 40 minutes because we hadn't worked this morning. We didn't begin on time this morning. But anyway, we're going to take a 50-minute break because that's what it said in the transcript, on the LiveNote. So a 50-minute lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, prior to the break we were just addressing, as you can recall, the VRS artillery campaign into the enclave, and you said in your evidence in response to Mr. Visnjic's question that UNPROFOR positions were not directly attacked by Bosnian Serb forces. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as my knowledge goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you have in fact used as part of your reference material the Dutch debriefing report, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if, for the purposes of the ELMO because it's in English, Prosecutor 404, tab 20, Madam Registrar. And Mr. Usher, if you could turn to page 22 of that report, and if you could move it down to paragraph 3.11. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I'll read this paragraph to you, 3.11: "In the early afternoon at around 1300 hours, two artillery shells exploded near to OP Foxtrot. Shortly afterwards, the OP came under direct fire from two Bosnian Serb army tanks. The tower of the observation post upon which the TOW anti-tank weapon was mounted was damaged. Through a liaison, the battalion requested an explanation from the Bosnian Serb army. However, the Bosnian Serb army required a written report of the incident probably as a stalling tactic."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Usher, if we could have 3.14, which is page 23, placed on the ELMO. 3.14, that's page 23. I think you have 3.17. It would be the page before. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: "On the morning of Saturday 8 July, the weather conditions were misty. There was only sporadic firing. At around 12.30 hours, the crew of OP Foxtrot reported that they were under fire. Shells were exploding at a short distance from the observation post. At 1345 hours, the observation post received a direct hit from a tank, and the right front side of the protective wall collapsed. A few minutes later, the wall received two more direct hits." Now, General, there are a number of other references in that report to direct attacks on UN observation posts which I won't refer you to, but you would agree with me that, based on this material, in fact the UN protection forces within the enclave did come under direct attack from the Bosnian Serb army, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with you in part. It is true that at one point they were in jeopardy; but that they were planned targets, had that been prepared, that would have -- they would have hit them in the first attempt. But yes, there was the risk of the war effects that I spoke about earlier on, and this is something that must be understood as the risk of war in a given area. But I still maintain that the UNPROFOR features were not planned military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're a military man. If something is directly hit, such as a tower from an observation post, wouldn't you agree with me that somebody would have to actually target that tower in order to hit it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could agree with you there. Of course, it can be hit by mistake or it can be targeted and hit as a result of the targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's move on, General, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 425. Page 14 of the English version, and for the General it would be page 11, the final page. Mr. Usher, if you could move the exhibit upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, this you will recall is the directive 7 signed by Radovan Karadzic, and in paragraph 6 of that document, he states support for combat operations, and the portion is highlighted on the ELMO. "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the International Community and international public opinion." Now, General, you would agree with me that this is, in fact, a directive from the Supreme Commander of the VRS to strangle resources available to UN Protection Forces within the enclaves of Gorazde and Zepa and, specifically in this case, of Srebrenica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps did not deal with those issues. It did not come under the competence of the Drina Corps, the permission or lack of it or reducing the entrance, restricting this. That was something that the Main Staff did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is not the question that I asked you. So I will repeat the question. I won't repeat the material. Would you agree with me, General, that that particular directive from the Supreme Commander of the VRS is a directive to strangle the resources available to UN Protection Forces within the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers rather to the superior support of UNPROFOR to the forces of the 28th Division because from the resources that were brought into the enclave, part of that was siphoned off to the funds of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the speakers and I have someone coming to look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll carry on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But, General, specifically this language actually refers to reducing and limiting the logistics support of UNPROFOR and the supply of resources to the Muslim population, does it not? It makes absolutely no reference to support for Muslim fighters within the enclaves, does it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in wars of the type carried on in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in and around Srebrenica, the army quite simply was in direct contact and closely integrated with the population with respect to the bases and supplies. And, unfortunately, and I say unfortunately, that too is a consequence of wars of this type which must be incorporated into our calculations when we consider the consequences of war and combat action. Unfortunately, that is something which naturally attends wars of this kind. It is not a specific feature of Srebrenica. It was something that was -- that happened on the whole -- the entire battlefield of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Where the army is, there you will find the population too. And if you wish to restrict the material resources of the army in the sense of combat resources, then you're also, by implication, restricting civilians, and this cannot be avoided. All that falls within the domain of what we refer to colloquially as collateral damage. Unfortunately, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you stated in your evidence-in-chief, and indeed I think within your report, that the UN Protection Forces did have sufficient material at its disposal to prevent the Krivaja 95 operation and compel the belligerents to respect the safe area. Now, you would agree with me that if the Bosnian Serbs were systematically strangling the resources that were available to the UN Protection Forces, the UN Protection Forces would be unable to defend the enclave, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand me properly. That's not what I thought, even if I said it. What I said was that UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina had the possibility of preventing operation Krivaja 95. Within the frameworks of the overall responsibility of UNPROFOR, the Dutch Battalion had to have prevented the actions of the 28th Division which triggered off the operation Krivaja 95. I did not mean to say that the Dutch Battalion should have opposed the VRS by fighting, by engaging in combat and to keep them within the enclave. What I thought was that it should have secured a strict respect for the May 1993 agreements with respect to demilitarisation and the absence of all forms of military activities from the enclave geared towards the VRS and then -- and it would have no reasons or arguments to launch a counter-offensive. As things stood, it gained the legitimate right of preventing military activities which were not prevented by the Dutch Battalion. And the Dutch Battalion for that mission, for its motion mission, did not only rely upon its own resources, but they had at their disposal the entire mechanism of the United Nations. So it was in that sense that I was addressing the portion of responsibility for that battalion, not that it did not engage in combat and stand up to the VRS in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the Dutch Battalion themselves within the enclave have sufficient resources to resist the Bosnian Serb advance into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor should they have resisted the Bosnian Serb army. They should have prevented the operation from taking place, and the best prevention would have been not to allow the 28th Division to violate the May 1993 agreements, and it had sufficient resources to be able to carry that through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you agree with me that the Bosnian Serb army essentially prevented military materiel from getting to UNPROFOR within the enclave by preventing convoys from entering the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it prevented this, if it did prevent it. I think that the convoys -- that the supply system of UNPROFOR was a highly elaborate one, and whether this happened at that period of time, I don't know. I have the testimony, I read it myself, but I do allow for the fact that there were restrictions in that respect. But as far as the Drina Corps was concerned, that wasn't its competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, Colonel Karremans, who was the commanding officer of the Dutch Battalion, testified in video-recorded testimony in this courtroom, and I won't read all of his evidence, but that in essence, the Bosnian Serb army prevented from entering the enclave replacement military personnel, military equipment, ammunition, food, spare parts for equipment. Now, you'd agree with me that the commanding officer of the Dutch Battalion would know better than you whether or not the Bosnian Serb army was preventing military materiel from getting into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would ask -- I would put the question in a different way, Mr. Cayley. Why did the battalion of the commander of the Dutch Battalion, why did he not, by the UN mechanism --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, answer my question, and I'll repeat it for you. If you don't want to answer it, just say, "I do not wish to answer." Would you agree with me, General, that the commanding officer of the Dutch Battalion would know better than you whether or not the Bosnian Serb army was preventing military materiel from getting into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I see in the transcript that the General has answered that question. That was his first word, and this was an addition, as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, you are saying that the General has already answered?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, line 24, page 63, the answer -- first word is the answer to the question, and after that we have the General's comment. Now, if Mr. Cayley isn't satisfied with the length of the answer, then that's another problem entirely; but if we're talking about whether he answered or not, I think he did answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are talking about line 24, are you talking about page 63, line 24? Is that it, "yes"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can move on, really. The General wanted me to formulate the question in a different way. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, are you aware that a threat was made to the Dutch Battalion that if there were further air strikes, that the Bosnian Serb army around Srebrenica would shell the Potocari compound and the surrounding area where there were located 25 to 30.000 civilians? Are you aware of that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read testimony to that -- statements to that effect, and the Dutch Battalion was a component part of the United Nations mechanism. At the point when, at their request, NATO planes launched strikes in the territory of Republika Srpska, then that Dutch Battalion sided with that warring party. That is the conclusion one reaches on the basis of all the rules and laws of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 77/18.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, you stated a moment ago that NATO, UNPROFOR forces, had at its disposal the necessary force to prevent further action, and in that one could refer to the air strikes. Now, the air strikes were made as a warning to the Bosnian Serbs. And in response - and I'll read this report, 77/18; this is an UNMO report - "The town is in the hands of the Bosnian Serb army by now and the latest ultimatum given by the Bosnian Serb army is that if the air strikes continue, everything inside the enclave will be bombed, also UNPROFOR and the other UN organisations." General, do you regard that as a lawful threat by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider it a threat, but not a lawful one, and luckily that threat was never acted upon, although NATO did act.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How could the Dutch Battalion defend all those people with that kind of threat hanging over them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in response to your question, I have answered several times: It is not -- it was not a threat when the operation was concluded. But they should have prevented the operation from taking place at all, and the Dutch Battalion, within the composition of the overall mechanism of the United Nations, including NATO which led the operation of the no-fly, denial-fly operation, had unlimited possibilities to prevent the operation from taking place. The Dutch Battalion did not perform its basic mission, that is, to secure the regime of demilitarisation in Srebrenica, and that is its fundamental error, its main mistake. It would have had to have done so, and that's where everything started.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could have Defence Exhibit 160, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, are you also aware - and in fact Colonel Karremans testified to this - that the Bosnian Serb army at the same time threatened to execute 32 Dutch UNPROFOR soldiers if the airstrikes continued? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I don't know about that threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Page 32. Now, General, I'll paraphrase paragraph 4.9 of your report, but in essence you say in that section of your report that "One undermanned battalion could not cushion the hatred of the Muslims towards the Serbs and vice versa," and then you state to the Secretary-General's report where it was acknowledged that the Dutch forces sent into Srebrenica were insufficient to do the job. So you yourself, in your report, accept the fact that the Dutch forces were woefully inadequate in order to meet the threat from outside, from the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. You didn't interpret the context of my assertion properly. In keeping with the UN Secretary-General's report pertaining to the military forces and options in the Security Council with respect to the scope of those forces that were to defend and protect the safe area, I took that into consideration, that is to say, what the UN Secretary-General says in his report, and that is that, when ascertaining the scope of the forces, everybody was convinced that they were insufficient, not strong enough to provide effective protection to the enclave. And I completely agree with him there because, first the Canadian company and then the Dutch Battalion, they were not forces that were sufficiently strong to defend the enclave if an operation were launched. So if we had to ensure a completely protected safe area, completely protected from all kinds of military activity from any side, including the VRS, then forces should have been sent which would have been capable by their fighting power, a real deterrent. They should have been a proper deterrent. And if an operation were launched that it would be a valid force capable of responding until the entire protection mechanism of the United Nations were unleashed and put into action. The mandate that was given to those forces was such that at any time new conflicts could have occurred, and that mandate and their force, their overall potential and strength were not a certain guarantee to prevent a conflict. And having given a mandate of that kind, then in front of them and behind them there should have been the authority of the United Nations to back them up and the overall political mechanism of supervision of the situation and the engagement of all the high representatives who existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia, from Zagreb to Tuzla, and that all -- had all of them performed their duties at the functions they performed, we probably wouldn't be here discussing this question today. That misfortune would have been averted and avoided. That is the sense of that paragraph. That is its meaning. It wasn't to generally condemn the Dutch Battalion. Of course, it was -- it did make an omission in failing to supervise the safe area regime and to inform its superiors of all the incidents, to take steps and to seek action. It did not do that. I do not say -- of course it is guilty for many of the activities from the beginning of the operation until the end of this whole sad episode, but we will probably hear that in another part of the testimony, but it made an omission. It failed to react to all violations of the regime of demilitarisation which was the cause for which operation Krivaja was planned, which led to the planning of the operation Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you so much, General. Let's move on to page 40 of your report in English, page 41 in the B/C/S. Could you read paragraph 6.3 of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I asked you if you could read portions of the text instead of me. I mean, if you want me to read this one I will do that for you, but I kindly asked you if it would be possible for you to read it out for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You need to save your voice, General. I can see that. I'll read it. "After establishing full control over Srebrenica, the VRS took all measures to ensure controlled evacuation of all those who wanted to be evacuated and to carry it out with the necessary and then feasible security measures." Do you stand by that statement, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; otherwise, I wouldn't have written it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm going to quote very briefly from General Dannatt -- Major-General Dannatt's testimony who you studied, the British divisional commander who testified before Their Honours, and he said the following in respect of a group of civilians who gathers in a small location which is occupied by a military force. This was his understanding as a divisional commander. He said: "Well, under the Geneva Conventions, the military are obliged to assume certain responsibilities for civilians when those civilians can no longer look after themselves. When their own civilian, municipal, or government structure can no longer look after them, then it falls to the military to carry out that function, and the minimum requirements of that function should be to provide food, water, shelter, and medical support." He then stated: "The status of those civilians under the Geneva Conventions becomes one of protected persons because, by definition, they can no longer protect themselves. They can no longer look after themselves. Therefore, from a military point of view, like it or not, then you have this duty of care which by the Geneva Convention is invested upon you and you must do the things I have just described; food, shelter, water, and medical care and freedom from harassment and the basic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. provisions of human rights." Now, General, a British divisional commander with operational experience gave that evidence before the Court. Do you agree with that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, of course I do. However, the context is completely different and the situation in point is completely different from the one which was analysed by General Dannatt quite legitimately. It is, of course, something that has to be applied if you have appropriate conditions to carry it out. But if you take an army such as was the VRS, which had one-half of a small pate as a daily ration for a soldier, that is the army which didn't have enough resources, didn't have enough logistics, but an army which was based on donations, which is quite ridiculous for an army that is engaged in warfare. Municipal authorities had an obligation to supply their soldiers, and they completely -- they were completely dependent on the goodwill of such authorities. I do not justify any ill-treatment towards civilians, whatever side they may be on, but unfortunately, once again, this is this most unfortunate consequence of any war. The civilians are the most vulnerable, the most exposed ones, despite the lofty formulations contained in relevant conventions. And such was the case in Bosnia and Herzegovina in general, and in particular, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And because they were vulnerable, General, is the very reason why armies have to take special care of civilians, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If they can; if they're able to do so. But one has to bear in mind the overall context. You cannot simply take it out of the context; you have to bear in mind the overall situation. First of all, it was a complete surprise for the VRS - that is, for an army which did not plan to liberate, or rather, take possession of the town - they were completely taken by surprise when such a large group, large number of civilians gathered. They were completely unprepared for that. Even if they had expected it, it is debatable as to whether they would be able to do so. You have a series of panicky orders issued by officers of the VRS when they learned about the initiatives to move out the civilian population. They had to collect a very high number of buses and other means of transport for that purpose, and it was very difficult to do that in such a short amount of time and in view of those consequences regarding the humanitarian crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, can you turn to paragraph 6.6 of your report on page -- I'm sorry, it is page 59 of your report and page 60 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 3.22. That's fine, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have that, General? It's the final sentence of paragraph 3.22. It's page 60. Do you have that in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I will read it: "All facts indicate that the commander of the Bosnian Serb Main Staff relieved the Drina Corps headquarters of the obligation to plan and carry out the operation of the movement of population from Srebrenica." That is your opinion, is it, in respect of the movement of the population out of the Srebrenica enclave, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only my opinion, it's a conclusion that I reached on the basis of everything that I had studied in that respect, including my personal contact with the people who were involved in the process, in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me that in order to move 25 to 30.000 people a distance, I think, of about 60 or 70 kilometres is quite a formidable task?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that it actually does require some kind of organisation, doesn't it? It doesn't just happen.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but here we're talking about an ad hoc kind of organisation, not a planned one. It would have been planned in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in order for an army to do it properly, it would need the involvement of the operation staff, of the transportation staff? They would at least have to be involved in some manner in order to organise this transport for 25.000 to 30.000 people.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only the army that took part in that. You have the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, the government, the United Nations mechanism, including Mr. Akashi, the Dutch Battalion. Everybody was involved in the execution of that task because it appeared suddenly, and it was a rather complex task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 436, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm not going to read this order out, but it is an order for the provision of buses, and it is an order to six of the Drina Corps brigades for the provision of buses. I think you yourself used this order to demonstrate what was taking place during the evacuation. General, who signs this order? Who is making the request for the buses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't signed by anyone, but I assume that it was signed in the original, and that is the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So General Zivanovic is ordering the buses for the movement of the population?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only the buses that were the property of his brigades. But there is also a request for buses issued by the Main Staff of the VRS, the Ministry of Defence, and the government of Republika Srpska. It was a general problem, not only the problem of the Drina Corps. And the first ones who were able to react were those who had the vehicles, that is, the brigades of the Drina Corps. So that was mobilised by the Corps Commander because he headed there immediately. That is the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- time that we see documents mentioning this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if the Drina Corps Commander is ordering buses for the evacuation of the population, it's completely incorrect, isn't it, to say that the VRS Main Staff relieved the Drina Corps headquarters of all obligations to carry out the operation for the movement of the population? That would be completely incorrect, wouldn't it, that assertion, based on this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. The Drina Corps had an obligation to activate part of its resources pursuant to the order of the Main Staff concerning the moving out of the population which had been agreed upon with the representatives of the civilian authorities, with the representatives of the Muslims from Srebrenica, and the United Nations mechanism. That operation was not within the competence of the Drina Corps; however, all of the resources were used because of the very brief period of time and a very critical humanitarian situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, evidence has been given by a Dutch officer before this courtroom that not only was General Zivanovic engaged in this operation, but also Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric, who was the chief of intelligence of the Drina Corps. Are you aware that Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric led the first convoy of civilians out of Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to your previous question, I stated, and I'm going to repeat that, the operation of the moving out of the civilian population from Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was not the responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you aware that Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric led out the first convoy of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, and this is the evidence of Witness B, a Dutch officer who was present at the two meetings in Bratunac on the 11th and 12th of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That witness identified Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric, a Drina Corps staff officer, as the man who led out the first convoy of civilians out of Potocari. Are you aware of that fact, General? That is the question that I want you to answer.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not familiar with that particular fact. But even if I did know that, it wouldn't affect the basic sense of my conclusion in any way. It was possible for any officer of the VRS to have led the first convoy out of the enclave, but the operation itself was the responsibility of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So at this point in time, General, we have two officers of the Drina Corps, the Commander and the Chief of Intelligence, one of whom who is proven by an order to have ordered buses, the other one led out the first convoy. Do you still maintain that the Drina Corps headquarters had been relieved of all obligations in respect of carrying out the movement of the population from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I still maintain that the Drina Corps headquarters were not involved in the operation. The staff of the Drina Corps at the time of that operation was involved in something completely different, that is, the preparation for the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 435, please. If that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, this is an intercepted radio communication dated the 12th of July between somebody called Krstic and Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic, and the conversation I will read goes as follows: "K: Hello, that Krsmanovic? X: Yes, go ahead. K: Listen! Write this down! X: Yes. K: Now: Pale, Visegrad, Rogatica, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Milici, Bratunac, Zvornik. Now: This, from all these places, 50 buses in total are to be at the stadium in Bratunac by 1700 hours. X: At 1700 hours at the Bratunac stadium. K: Very sure this is done! Is that clear? X: Understood. K: Go ahead."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This exhibit is bis, I'm just told. I'm sorry. So 435 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, this is an intercepted radio communication in which General Krstic is requesting the chief of transportation of the Drina Corps to organise 50 buses. Now, you would agree with me, if General Zivanovic, General Krstic, Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric, and Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic were all involved in this operation to move 30.000 people out of Srebrenica, it is completely incorrect to suggest to this Court that the Drina Corps headquarters had been relieved of all obligations to plan and carry out the operation to remove the population from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot tell me what to say. You cannot put my answer to me. What I'm telling you is that - and this has been testified to on several occasions before this Chamber - that at the time the operation of the moving out of the civilian population from Srebrenica was carried out, the Drina Corps was engaged in the planning, organisation of a new operation, namely, the Stupcanica 95 operation. In view of the fact of what is required when preparing and planning an operation, and I know that that operation was planned, I claim and I'm convinced -- I'm firmly convinced that the Drina Corps, that is that the Drina Corps staff, the command, could not take part in the organisation of this particular operation. At the meeting which was held in the evening of the 11th at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, which was chaired by the Commander of the Main Staff, the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps was tasked with planning and preparing the Zepa operation. For me as a military expert, it is a sufficient reason to conclude that, from that moment on, Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps cannot have any other duty if he's already appointed commander of the operational group. All he can busy himself with was to plan that operation and to prepare for its execution. And in response to a question which was put to me by the Defence counsel as regards what that implies, I think I already said what it implies, what it includes. I can repeat once again what I said. One person cannot be at two places at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're not answering my question. I'm not going to let you talk forever. General, do you accept that if four officers of the Drina headquarters -- if evidence has been provided to this Court that four officers of the Drina Corps Command were involved in the organisation of buses for the movement of the population, then it is completely incorrect to suggest that the Drina Corps had no involvement in the movement of the population out of Srebrenica. If you do not want to answer this question, then simply say, "I decline to answer."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I will give you my answer. If you think that I am particularly willing of talking all the time, then you're wrong because I'm quite tired by now, but I will say once again I have already stated - I have stated now and I will state it tomorrow, until the date I die - that any staff which receives an obligation, a duty to plan and organise a military operation cannot be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, it's the Presiding Judge that's interrupting you now. You're an intelligent person, General. The question was a simple one. You're an expert witness. You're providing us with expert testimony. You know what it means. And you're a military expert. So you are here to comment also on hypotheses. The question is as follows: Imagine there's evidence according to which two or three officers of the Drina Corps had taken part in the organisation and in the provision of buses. Do you still stand by your claim, the one that you expressed in your report, that the Drina Corps was entirely relieved of this duty to organise transport? It's a very simple question. The question is, if this is true, do you still stand by your statement? So, just tell us, "Yes, I still stand by my statement," or, "I don't stand by what I said on a previous occasion." Please, give us a direct answer and be mindful of the strain for your throat. Mr. Cayley, could you repeat once again your question. Could you put it very precisely. And I appeal to you, General, once again, to give us a straightforward answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, the Court has heard evidence that at least four members of the Drina Corps headquarters, including General Krstic, were personally involved in the organisation of transport to remove the civilian population from Srebrenica. On that basis, would you agree with me that it is incorrect, your assertion, that the Drina Corps headquarters had been relieved of all obligations to plan and carry out the operation of the movement of the population from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation I received was to remove. Maybe we do not have an equivalent in our language. The issue was not that of a removal, but of the movement of the population out of a certain place. There is a significant difference between the two expressions. I apologise for this digression, but let me answer your question now. The command of the Drina Corps did not plan and it did not execute this operation. Of course, the operation was conducted in its area of responsibility, and portions of its resources, as it can be seen from the order of the Corps commander, did take part in it. The assistant commander for logistics or the chief of transportation are not members of the staff, Mr. Prosecutor. They are members of the rear elements of the Drina Corps command and not the members of the staff. Is my answer precise enough, because I really do wish to be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, thank you very much for trying, General. Mr. Cayley, sorry to interrupt you, but I think that we will have to wind up for the day and continue on Monday. We will reconvene on Monday, 9.20. General, please take advantage of the weekend that is before you to have some rest. Yes, Mr. Cayley, is there anything that you would like to add at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps not the best time to state this on a Friday afternoon, but I suspect that I may actually be going longer than all day Monday. I may have to go into Tuesday, but I will try to get through it as quickly as possible. It is problematic for the reasons I think that we all understand, but I will try to move as quick as I can, but I don't guarantee that I will finish by the end of Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask Madam Registrar to make a calculation of the time which was spent on the examination. We have to bear in mind the questions of the Judges as well, so I will ask Madam Registrar to give us information on that, and on Monday I will be in a better position to inform you thereof. Have a nice weekend, all of you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of December, 2000, at 9.20 a.m. 25
